decision_reason: The closest unseen pair, exercising on a stepper versus cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions, differs only in cadence in A1. Adding gravity-relative thigh inclination offers a posture-based contrast transferable from sitting, standing and horizontal cycling. A lateral posture attribute addresses the nearly identical lying prototypes without relying on their questionable smoothness difference. Intensity variability provides a transferable description of intermittent basketball and elevator movement, complementing their relatively weak seen coverage. Elevator travel direction, sustained velocity and machine-specific movement details are not introduced because their reliable observability is not established.

attributes.name: motion_intensity
attributes.definition: Overall magnitude and energy of motion within a window, including both linear and rotational components.

attributes.name: cadence
attributes.definition: Rate at which a meaningful periodic motion unit repeats over time. Cadence measures repetitions per unit time, not the total number of repetitions in the recording.

levels.Low: No clear periodic repetition or a slow repetition rate.

attributes.name: smoothness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion changes continuously rather than through sustained rapid fluctuations.

levels.Medium: Moderately smooth motion with some fluctuations.
levels.High: Continuous and smooth motion with little fluctuation.

attributes.name: impulsiveness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion contains short, abrupt, high-magnitude changes or impacts.

levels.Low: Few or no pronounced abrupt peaks.

attributes.name: posture_inclination
attributes.definition: Average gravity-relative inclination of the global load-bearing body configuration within a window, rather than the orientation of an isolated moving limb.

levels.High: Strongly inclined or nearly horizontal relative to gravity.

attributes.name: posture_variability
attributes.definition: Extent to which the global load-bearing body configuration changes relative to gravity within a window, rather than local limb-orientation changes.

attributes.name: rotational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of angular or rotational motion during the activity.

attributes.name: translational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of sustained linear progression or locomotor translation within a window.

levels.High: Prominent sustained translational or locomotor motion.

attributes.name: motion_regularity
attributes.definition: Temporal consistency and predictability of the motion pattern.

levels.Low: Irregular and poorly predictable motion pattern.
levels.Medium: Partly structured motion with moderate variability.

attributes.name: thigh_inclination
attributes.definition: Typical inclination of the thighs' long axes away from the gravity vertical within a window, considering both legs rather than isolated peak excursions.

levels.Low: Thighs remain predominantly close to vertical.
levels.Medium: Thighs have intermediate typical inclination away from vertical.
levels.High: Thighs remain predominantly close to horizontal.

attributes.name: lateral_posture_inclination
attributes.definition: Degree to which the body's anatomical left-right axis is aligned with gravity, distinguishing side-oriented posture from upright or back-oriented posture.

levels.Low: The body's left-right axis is nearly perpendicular to gravity.
levels.Medium: The body's left-right axis is oblique to gravity.
levels.High: The body's left-right axis is nearly parallel to gravity.

attributes.name: intensity_variability
attributes.definition: Extent of changes in the local magnitude of motion over a window, distinct from mean intensity, isolated impact sharpness and repetition timing.

levels.Low: Motion magnitude remains nearly constant, whether weak or strong.
levels.Medium: Motion magnitude shows moderate changes over time.
levels.High: Motion magnitude shows pronounced changes between quieter and more active intervals.

operations.reason: motion_intensity: G3 supports overall acceleration and rotation magnitude across torso and limbs. This retains a broad transfer axis from quiet standing to vigorous running and jumping. Resistance, technique and individual effort can blur adjacent levels; intensity alone should not distinguish stepper from cross trainer.
seen_anchors: running on a treadmill with a speed of 8 km/h

operations.reason: cadence: G6 supports repetition rate in leg and arm motion. It preserves the existing stepper-versus-cycling contrast and transfers from walking and horizontal cycling. Exercise pace is not fixed by these class names, and pauses or harmonic ambiguity can obscure the meaningful repetition rate.
target_unseen: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions
contrast_unseen: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)
cycling on an exercise bike in horizontal positions

operations.reason: smoothness: G9 supports sustained rapid changes in torso and limb signals, contrasting continuous exercise with fluctuating locomotion. Transfers from cross trainer and jumping are plausible. Impacts and sensor movement can reduce apparent smoothness; no reliable smoothness difference is implied between the two lying postures.

impulsiveness: G10 supports brief abrupt changes associated with foot contact and landing, providing transfer from walking and jumping to stair descent and basketball. Soft landings, surface compliance and sensor attachment affect peak prominence. Elevator start or stop transients are possible but are not guaranteed within a window.

posture_inclination: G1 supports mean gravity-relative torso and whole-body configuration. It retains transfer from upright standing and reclined cycling to vertical cycling. Dynamic acceleration, trunk lean and ambiguity in the exercise-position labels limit precise ordinal assignment; limb orientation alone must not determine this attribute.
target_unseen: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions
seen_anchors: cycling on an exercise bike in horizontal positions

operations.reason: posture_variability: G12 supports changes in gravity-relative torso and global body configuration. Rowing and walking provide seen examples of changing posture, relevant to basketball and elevator movement. Isolated arm or leg excursions must not be mistaken for global posture changes, and brief windows may contain only one posture.

rotational_motion: G2 supports angular motion of instrumented limbs and torso. Horizontal cycling and cross trainer provide transferable examples for vertical cycling and stepper exercise. Large limb rotations need not imply trunk turning, and this broad attribute cannot reliably identify a particular machine trajectory.
target_unseen: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions
seen_anchors: cycling on an exercise bike in horizontal positions

operations.reason: translational_motion: G13 supports short-window translation proxies, retaining a useful distinction between progressing locomotion and stationary exercise. Walking supplies a seen anchor for stair descent and basketball. Constant elevator velocity is not directly observable from inertial acceleration, and treadmill locomotion is not equivalent to world-frame displacement; these remain limitations rather than reasons to add a travel-direction attribute.
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)

operations.reason: motion_regularity: G6 and G11 support recurrence and temporal predictability. Structured treadmill exercise and less constrained outdoor walking anchor comparisons with machine exercise, elevator movement and basketball. Short windows can make irregular activities appear repetitive; regularity does not require constant motion amplitude.
seen_anchors: running on a treadmill with a speed of 8 km/h

operations.reason: thigh_inclination: G1 supports gravity-relative leg orientation, with G12 indicating variation during the movement. Seated pedaling generally keeps thighs more elevated than weight-bearing stepping, adding a posture-based contrast to the low-U_NN stepper/vertical-cycling pair rather than another rate attribute. Sitting, standing and horizontal cycling provide seen support. Leg-sensor anatomical alignment, dynamic acceleration, step height and bicycle setup can blur levels, so separation is expected rather than guaranteed.
target_unseen: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions
contrast_unseen: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions
seen_anchors: cycling on an exercise bike in horizontal positions

operations.reason: lateral_posture_inclination: G1 supports gravity alignment of the torso's anatomical lateral axis. It adds a clear physical distinction between lying on back and lying on right side, whose A1 prototypes differ only in smoothness, and supplies a complementary posture axis for interpreting upright unseen activities. Prediction requires consistent anatomical sensor alignment; dynamic lateral acceleration and transient leaning can obscure posture. It does not distinguish right-side from left-side lying.
target_unseen: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions

operations.reason: intensity_variability: G4 supports changes in motion magnitude over time. Quiet-to-active transitions in torso and limb motion offer a transferable description for weakly covered basketball and moving around in an elevator, using sustained running and outdoor walking as seen anchors. This differs from mean energy, repetition timing and single sharp impacts. A window containing only steady play or one elevator maneuver may miss the variability, so high variability is not guaranteed for every window.
seen_anchors: running on a treadmill with a speed of 8 km/h

semantic_redundancy_review: The twelve attributes retain distinct physical scopes. Motion intensity describes average magnitude; intensity variability describes changes in magnitude; impulsiveness describes short abrupt peaks; smoothness describes sustained rapid fluctuation. Cadence measures repetition rate, whereas motion regularity measures predictability. Global posture inclination and its variability exclude isolated limb orientation; thigh inclination deliberately captures that separate segment-level configuration. Lateral posture inclination resolves a direction of gravity alignment that total inclination loses. Rotational and translational motion describe different movement components, subject to inertial observability limits. Correlation is expected but is not treated as equivalence. No machine identity, elevator direction, ball contact, mandatory arm action or guaranteed prototype separation is encoded.
